title: The General Who Ran Out of Time
subtitle: The man who planned D-Day and ran a superpower had one rule about time. Thirty-five years later, someone turned it into four boxes.

card.essence: He commanded the largest sea invasion in history and then ran the United States. His secret was not doing more — it was knowing what could wait.

intention: you'll learn where the famous urgent/important grid really came from, use it to sort six real-life tasks, and practise the language of obligation: must, have to, need to, don't have to, needn't.
warmup: What did you do first this morning — the most important thing, or the most urgent one?
Is your phone a tool that helps you, or a boss that interrupts you?
Think of something important in your life that you keep putting off. Why is it so easy to delay?

trivial — “We spent an hour arguing about a trivial detail.”

story.heading: Part 1 — A storm in June
paras: In the spring of 1944, General Dwight D. Eisenhower had one of the hardest jobs in history. He was the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, and he was responsible for Operation Overlord — the invasion of Nazi-occupied France. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, thousands of ships and aircraft, and millions of tons of supplies all depended on his decisions.

The invasion was planned for 5 June. But the weather turned terrible, and Eisenhower had to postpone it. Then his weather experts told him there might be a short break in the storm. He listened, asked questions, and finally gave the order to go. On 6 June, D-Day, the landings began.

In his pocket, Eisenhower carried a short note he had written in case the invasion failed. It said that the decision had been his, and that “any blame or fault” belonged to him alone. He never needed it. But the note shows something about the man: he knew which decisions only he could make — and he made them.
checks: Why was the invasion moved from 5 June to 6 June?
What did Eisenhower's secret note say?
answers: The Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied France in 1944.
Because of terrible weather; the experts predicted a short break in the storm.
That the decision was his, and that if the invasion failed, all the blame was his alone.
story.discuss: Eisenhower wrote the note before he knew the result. What does that tell you about him as a leader?

story.heading: Part 2 — Two kinds of problems
paras: After the war, Eisenhower spent several years as president of Columbia University in New York, and in 1953 he became President of the United States. His days were full of pressing problems, and he was known for protecting his time. He wanted short, clear reports and trusted his staff to deal with anything they could handle themselves.

In August 1954, he gave a speech in Evanston, near Chicago. In it, he quoted what he called the words of “a former college president”: “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.”

Nobody is completely sure who that college president was. Some people point to a university leader Eisenhower knew; others notice that Eisenhower himself had recently been one. Either way, the idea stayed with him. Some of his greatest achievements — the national highway system and the creation of NASA — were not emergencies. They were important projects that took years of patient planning.
checks: Which university did Eisenhower lead after the war?
According to the quotation, what is the relationship between urgent and important problems?
Why were the highways and NASA good examples of his idea?
answers: Columbia University in New York — he was its president.
Urgent problems are usually not important, and important problems are rarely urgent.
They weren't emergencies — they were important long-term projects that needed years of planning.
story.discuss: Do you agree that the important things are “never urgent”? Can you think of an exception?

story.heading: Part 3 — From a sentence to four boxes
paras: For decades, Eisenhower's sentence was simply a good quotation. Then, in 1989, the American writer Stephen Covey published The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, which became one of the best-selling business books ever. In it, Covey made the idea famous as a grid: urgent or not urgent along one side, important or not important along the other. Four boxes. Over time, people began calling it the Eisenhower Matrix.
The grid gives each box an action. Urgent and important: do it now. Important but not urgent: schedule it. Urgent but not important: delegate it, if you can. Neither: drop it.

Covey's big point was about the second box. Exercise, learning, relationships, planning — these things are never urgent, so we procrastinate until they become emergencies. An American writer, Charles Hummel, had already given the problem a name in 1967: the tyranny of the urgent. Today, with a phone that buzzes every few minutes, that tyranny may be stronger than ever.
checks: Which book made the four-box grid famous, and when?
What should you do with a task that is urgent but not important?
Why does Covey think the “important, not urgent” box is the most dangerous?
answers: Stephen Covey's 1989 book, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People.
Delegate it — give it to someone else, if possible.
Because nothing forces us to do those tasks, so we keep delaying them until they become emergencies.
story.discuss: The grid is named after Eisenhower, but Covey made it famous. Who deserves the credit?

tool_tab.lead: Two questions, four boxes. Across the bottom: how urgent is it — does it need attention now? Up the side: how important is it — does it matter for your goals and values? Each box has its own action.
how: Write down everything on your mind — work, home, people, ideas.
Ask the importance question first: does this help my goals or the people I care about? Only then ask: must it happen soon?
Put each task in a box. Be honest: most people put far too much in “do it now”.
Act box by box: do, schedule (with a real time in your calendar), delegate, or drop — and don't feel guilty about dropping.

sort.intro: Which box does each task belong in? Choose, then check.

items.text: Scrolling through random videos on your phone before bed.
items.why: no deadline and no real value — drop it.

items.text: Your child has a high temperature and needs to see a doctor this afternoon.
items.why: health and family, and it can't wait — do it now.

items.text: Starting regular exercise so that you stay healthy in ten years' time.
items.why: it matters a lot, but nothing forces you to start today — schedule it.

items.text: The report your boss needs by 5 p.m. today — and a big client is waiting for it.
items.why: a real deadline with real consequences — do it now.

items.text: A colleague keeps asking you to book meeting rooms — a quick job that anyone in the team could do.
items.why: it feels urgent but doesn't need you — delegate it.

items.text: Planning where you want your career to be in five years.
items.why: very important, never urgent — put a time in the calendar.

breaks: Not everyone can delegate. The grid assumes you have someone to hand work to. A student, a parent or a small-business owner often doesn't.
Whose importance? Your boss's “important” and yours may be very different.
Life isn't a list. Some of the best moments — a long talk with a friend — look like “neither” on paper.
discuss: Which box do you spend most of your time in? Which do you wish you spent more time in?
Is there anything in your life that the grid would call “drop it” that you would never drop?

grammar.name: must, have to, need to, don't have to
grammar.lead: Sorting tasks is really a question of obligation: what must happen, what we don't have to do at all. English has several ways to say this, and the differences matter.
notes:
must — strong obligation, often from the speaker (a personal rule or strong advice).
“I must call my grandmother this week — it's been too long.”

have to — obligation from outside: rules, laws, other people.
“Pilots have to retire at a certain age.”  Past: “We had to wait two hours at the border.” (must has no past form.)

need to — something is necessary to reach a goal.
“You need to book early if you want a window seat.”

don't have to / don't need to / needn't — it isn't necessary; you can choose.
“You don't have to bring anything — we have plenty of food.”

mustn't — it is NOT allowed, or a very bad idea. It is not the opposite of must!
“You mustn't use your phone while you're driving.”

exercises.heading: Choose the right form
exercises.intro: Write must, mustn't, have to, had to or don't have to in each gap. Use each once.
items: 1. It's Saturday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early. I can sleep until ten.
2. Yesterday the train was cancelled and I ___ take a taxi.
3. In many countries, drivers ___ wear a seat belt — it's the law.
4. This is a secret. You ___ tell anyone.
5. I really ___ stop eating so much chocolate — I've told myself a hundred times.

exercises.heading: Same meaning or different?
items: 1. You don't have to pay. / You needn't pay. → ___
2. You mustn't touch it. / You don't have to touch it. → ___
3. We need to leave by six. / We have to leave by six. → ___
4. She had to work late. / She must work late. → ___
answers: 2. different — the first is forbidden; the second is only unnecessary.
4. different — the first is in the past; the second is about now or the future.

grammar.closing: Now describe your own week with the grid: one thing you have to do, one you need to schedule, and one you don't have to do at all.

speak.intro: Use the matrix on your own life. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “That goes in the … box, because …” · “I don't have to … — someone else could.” · “I really need to make time for …” · “It feels urgent, but it isn't important.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your real week
paras: Name four things on your mind this week and put one in each box. Which box was hardest to fill?

tasks.label: Task 2 — The neglected box
paras: What is one “important, not urgent” thing you keep postponing? What would it take to start this month?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Advice
paras: Someone you know is overwhelmed. Explain the matrix to them in two minutes, using an example from their life.

final: Eisenhower wrote his “blame” note before D-Day. Which decisions in your life can only you make?
Are phones and notifications making the tyranny of the urgent worse — or can technology help us escape it?
Is it ever right to do something unimportant first? When?
From memory: make four sentences about Eisenhower's story with had to, needed to, didn't have to and mustn't.
